title: Sodium Batteries Hit a Tesla-Level Milestone — But There's a Chilly Problem
summary: A sodium-ion battery from Chinese manufacturer Hina has achieved a surprising feat: it's on par with Tesla's lithium-ion cells in terms of manufacturing uniformity and high-power performance. That's the key takeaway from a study published in Cell Reports Physical Science, where researchers at RWTH Aachen University in Germany put 120 Hina cells through a gauntlet of tests. The findings suggest sodium-ion technology — which uses abundant, cheap sodium instead of costly lithium — could soon become a viable alternative for electric vehicles and grid storage. But there's a catch: the battery performs poorly when charged at low temperatures, and an unexpected discovery inside the cathode has scientists scratching their heads. The team used impedance spectroscopy, a non-destructive method that measures how uniform a battery's internal structure is. "We were positively surprised by how uniform the cells are," said Moritz Schütte, the study's lead researcher. Uniformity is crucial for battery life and safety, and the Hina cells matched the consistency seen in Tesla's industry-leading designs. The battery even shares a key architectural feature with Tesla: a tabless, double-aluminum current collector that reduces electrical resistance and evens out temperature distribution. When tested across a range of currents and temperatures from -20°C to 45°C, the sodium cells delivered impressive high-power output — better than expected for an early commercial product. However, charging below freezing was a clear weakness. "For applications that require frequent charging at low ambient temperatures, appropriate thermal management or operating strategies will be important," Schütte noted. That limits the battery's immediate use in cold-climate EVs without a battery warmer. The team also dissected the cells and used X-rays to examine their inner structure. They found unusually high and unevenly distributed copper concentrations in parts of the cathode. Copper isn't typically part of the cathode chemistry, so its presence "raises interesting questions about its role in performance and aging," Schütte said. It could be a contaminant or a deliberate additive — the team isn't sure yet. Despite the cold-weather hurdle, the results are a major boost for sodium-ion technology. Sodium is the sixth most abundant element on Earth, found in seawater and salt deposits, so it sidesteps the supply chain and cost issues that plague lithium. Schütte envisions these batteries first powering stationary storage systems and short-range commercial vehicles, where cost matters more than maximum range. The next step? Making the cells charge safely and efficiently below 0°C. If researchers crack that, your future electric car might run on salt.
why_it_matters: Sodium-ion batteries could lower the cost of electric cars and grid storage, reducing our dependence on scarce lithium and making clean energy more accessible globally — but their cold-weather limitation might delay their use in northern regions unless solved.

background_read: Most electric vehicles today run on lithium-ion batteries, but lithium is scarce, expensive to mine, and concentrated in a few countries, raising supply concerns. Sodium, by contrast, is the sixth most abundant element on Earth — found in seawater and salt deposits — making sodium-ion batteries a potentially cheaper and more sustainable alternative. In 2020, Tesla unveiled its innovative 'tabless' 4680 battery cell, which reduced internal resistance and improved heat distribution, setting a new industry standard for uniformity. RWTH Aachen University (Rheinisch-Westfälische Technische Hochschule, a leading engineering research institution in Germany) conducted the rigorous tests on 120 Hina cells, comparing them directly to Tesla's benchmark. The results show that sodium-ion technology is approaching commercial viability, but the poor cold-weather charging means extra heating systems would be needed for electric cars in colder climates.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Sodium-ion battery from Hina matches Tesla's lithium-ion cells in uniformity and high-power performance.
└─ BUT: Performs poorly when charged at low temperatures, and mysterious copper was found in the cathode.
RESEARCH METHOD: 120 Hina cells tested by RWTH Aachen University using impedance spectroscopy — a non-destructive way to measure internal uniformity.
├─ FINDING 1: Uniformity matches Tesla's tabless design; the battery shares a tabless, double-aluminum current collector that reduces resistance.
└─ FINDING 2: Impressive high-power output across a range of currents and temperatures (from -20°C to 45°C), but charging below freezing is a clear weakness requiring thermal management.
UNEXPECTED DISCOVERY: X-rays and dissection revealed high, unevenly distributed copper in the cathode — possibly a contaminant or a deliberate additive with an unclear role in performance and aging.
IMPLICATIONS: Major boost for sodium-ion viability in stationary energy storage and short-range vehicles; the cold-weather hurdle must be solved before widespread use in electric cars.
OPEN QUESTION: How to enable safe, efficient charging below 0°C? And what is the copper doing, and can it be controlled?

perspectives.description: Sodium is cheap and abundant everywhere, so these batteries could slash battery prices, shorten supply chains, and avoid the environmental damage of lithium mining. If manufacturing scales up, clean energy storage could become affordable even in poorer countries, accelerating the shift away from fossil fuels.

The poor charging performance in cold weather is a serious drawback for electric vehicles in much of North America, Europe, and Asia. Adding battery warmers adds cost and complexity, and the unexplained copper contamination might signal long-term reliability issues that could delay adoption until fully understood.

The study marks an important technological stepping stone: sodium-ion cells can now match lithium-ion in key manufacturing metrics. The unexpected copper find, while puzzling, could open new research paths into how battery chemistries age and how we design future cells. It's a reminder that innovation often uncovers new questions alongside solutions.

If researchers crack the cold-charging problem and clarify copper's role, sodium-ion batteries could first dominate stationary storage and then move into mass-market EVs. This might reshape the global battery industry, reduce geopolitically sensitive lithium dependencies, and make electric transportation more accessible within the next decade.
